comments.text:
Crisis, Compliance, and Extraction. Across history, governments have treated crises the same way a manipulative lover treats suspicion: as an opportunity. A moment of panic becomes a moment of power. War, economic collapse, political conflict, it doesn’t matter. The formula never changes. When people are afraid, governments tighten their grip, raise the cost of living, and extract more wealth from the very citizens they claim to protect. And the cruel part? The extraction never ends when the crisis does.

War is the state’s favorite excuse. During the U.S. Civil War, the government didn’t just fight a rebellion, it used the chaos to slip in the first national income tax. Once the door was open, it never closed. By World War II, the tax system had mutated into something monstrous: taxpayers skyrocketed from 4 million to 43 million, and top rates hit 94%. Inflation and rationing quietly drained wallets while politicians pretended it was patriotic sacrifice.

The Korean War piled on an Excess Profits Tax, 82% on wartime corporate gains. Vietnam brought inflation so brutal that prices more than doubled between 1965 and 1980. Citizens watched their purchasing power evaporate while the state shrugged and called it “policy.”

Every conflict becomes a fiscal opportunity.  
Every emergency becomes a justification.  
Every citizen becomes the collateral.

And even when governments don’t create crises, they weaponize them.

After the Civil War, temporary tax structures magically became permanent. After World War II, top tax rates stayed at 91% for more than a decade, justified by Cold War paranoia. Bretton Woods locked nations into monetary constraints that gave governments the perfect excuse to tighten fiscal controls and raise taxes under the guise of “stability.”

Crises don’t just expand state power.  
They reconstruct it.

This pattern isn’t modern, it’s ancestral. Colonial empires perfected the art of crisis extraction. Britain entered the Seven Years’ War drowning in debt, then turned around and squeezed the colonies with the Sugar Act, Stamp Act, and Townshend Acts. Paper, sugar, glass, tea, everything became a revenue stream. The colonists didn’t choose the war, but they paid for it. The pressure helped ignite the American Revolution.

Governments provoke conflict, escalate conflict, or simply wait for conflict, because conflict is profitable.

Economic collapse works just as well.  
During the Great Depression, the U.S. government rolled out the New Deal, funded by new taxes. The Social Security payroll tax began at a “modest” 2%, but it permanently increased the cost of labor and reduced take‑home pay. Excise taxes on gasoline, alcohol, and tobacco rose, quietly inflating the cost of everyday life. Recovery was the excuse. Extraction was the reality.

External pressure? Same story.

After World War I, Germany was crushed under 132 billion gold marks in reparations. The government printed money until hyperinflation devoured the nation. Prices doubled every 3.7 days. Citizens watched their savings disintegrate while the state used inflation to shrink its debt.

In the late 20th century, IMF structural adjustment programs forced countries to raise taxes, cut subsidies, and increase prices on essentials. Modern sanctioned states, Iran, Venezuela, North Korea, repeatedly raise domestic prices or impose new taxes to compensate for lost revenue.

Citizens didn’t cause the crisis.  
Citizens still pay for it.

This is the part that stings, the betrayal that feels personal once you see it clearly:

Crisis creates compliance.  
Compliance enables extraction.  
Extraction becomes permanent.

War, depression, colonial conflict, sanctions, the details change, but the architecture doesn’t. Governments expand their fiscal reach when people are scared, distracted, or desperate. And once the state takes more, it never gives it back.

Across centuries, the pattern is brutally consistent:  
The state survives by extracting from its citizens.  
And the citizens pay the price long after the crisis ends.
